title: What is the difference between severity (the technical/business IMPACT of a defect) and priority (how URGENTLY it must be fixed), and why can a defect be low-severity but high-priority (e.g. a company-logo typo on the landing page) or high-severity but low-priority (a crash in a rarely-used admin edge case)?
shortTitle: Severity vs priority, and why they can diverge

s1_definition.profdef: Severity is the degree of technical and business impact a defect has on the system, how badly it breaks functionality, data, or safety, and it is usually judged by the tester or by the nature of the bug. Priority is how urgently the defect must be fixed relative to other work, judged by the product owner or business based on customer, revenue, reputational, and scheduling factors. They are independent axes, so a defect can be any combination of high or low on each: a defect can be low-severity but high-priority, such as a misspelled company name on the landing page, or high-severity but low-priority, such as a crash in a rarely used admin edge case affecting one internal user.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, severity is "how much damage does this bug do?" and priority is "how soon must we fix it?" A typo in the bank's name splashed across the public homepage does almost no technical damage, so it is low severity, but it embarrasses the brand in front of every visitor, so the business wants it fixed within the hour, making it high priority. On the other hand, a rare crash deep inside an admin screen that only one back-office clerk ever opens is technically a serious crash, high severity, but because almost nobody hits it and there is a manual workaround, the business is fine fixing it next sprint, making it low priority.
s1_definition.oneliner: Severity measures how badly a defect damages the system, priority measures how urgently it must be fixed, and because impact and urgency are different axes a bug can be low-severity high-priority, like a homepage typo, or high-severity low-priority, like a crash in a rarely used admin corner.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Severity is the degree of technical and business impact a defect has on the system, how badly it breaks functionality, data, or safety, and it is usually judged by the tester or by the nature of the bug. Priority is how urgently the defect must be fixed relative to other work, judged by the product owner or business based on customer, revenue, reputational, and scheduling factors. They are independent axes, so a defect can be any combination of high or low on each: a defect can be low-severity but high-priority, such as a misspelled company name on the landing page, or high-severity but low-priority, such as a crash in a rarely used admin edge case affecting one internal user.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, severity is "how much damage does this bug do?" and priority is "how soon must we fix it?" A typo in the bank's name splashed across the public homepage does almost no technical damage, so it is low severity, but it embarrasses the brand in front of every visitor, so the business wants it fixed within the hour, making it high priority. On the other hand, a rare crash deep inside an admin screen that only one back-office clerk ever opens is technically a serious crash, high severity, but because almost nobody hits it and there is a manual workaround, the business is fine fixing it next sprint, making it low priority.

**One line to remember:** Severity measures how badly a defect damages the system, priority measures how urgently it must be fixed, and because impact and urgency are different axes a bug can be low-severity high-priority, like a homepage typo, or high-severity low-priority, like a crash in a rarely used admin corner.

sections.s2_technical:
Severity is primarily a technical judgement about the defect itself. A crash, data corruption, a wrong monetary calculation, or a security hole are high severity because they damage core functionality, correctness, or safety. A cosmetic misalignment, a non-blocking warning, or a minor label issue is low severity because the system still works correctly. Teams usually define severity levels such as critical, major, minor, and trivial, with objective criteria so testers can classify consistently. Severity tends to be set by whoever finds and analyzes the bug, because it reflects the nature of the failure.

Priority is a business and scheduling judgement about when to fix it. It weighs how many users are affected, whether there is a workaround, the revenue or compliance impact, reputational risk, the release schedule, and what else is competing for developer time. Priority is usually set by the product owner or triage group, often in collaboration with the tester. The same defect can have its priority raised or lowered as business context changes, for example a bug becomes high priority the week before a major launch.

The two diverge because impact and urgency are different questions. The classic low-severity, high-priority case is a typo in the company name or a wrong logo on the public landing page: technically nothing is broken, the system works perfectly, so severity is low, yet every visitor sees an embarrassing brand mistake, so the business demands an immediate fix, making priority high. The classic high-severity, low-priority case is a crash in a rarely used administrative edge case: a crash is a serious failure, so severity is high, but perhaps only one internal user ever triggers it, a manual workaround exists, and no customer or money is affected, so the business is comfortable scheduling it for a later sprint, making priority low. Other combinations are common too: a high-severity high-priority bug is a transfer that debits the wrong amount, fix now; a low-severity low-priority bug is a cosmetic misalignment on a seldom-visited settings page, fix whenever convenient.

The senior nuances are these. First, keep the axes separate in your tracker with two distinct fields, because conflating them leads to poor triage, either polishing cosmetic issues while serious bugs wait, or ignoring a scary-sounding bug that does not actually matter. Second, severity informs priority but does not determine it; the business decides priority using severity as one input among many. Third, always capture a workaround and the affected user population in the bug report, because those are exactly the facts that let a product owner set priority correctly. Fourth, be ready in an interview to defend a surprising combination with a concrete example, because that is how an interviewer checks you truly understand the distinction rather than treating the two words as synonyms.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's public homepage shows the bank name misspelled. Nothing is technically broken, but every visitor sees it, so the brand team wants it fixed immediately. The bank needs a way to record that this defect has low technical impact but high business urgency. This is exactly a low-severity, high-priority defect.

Problem 2 — A crash occurs in a rarely used admin report that one back-office clerk opens once a month, and there is a manual workaround. The crash is technically serious but almost nobody hits it. This is exactly a high-severity, low-priority defect.

Problem 3 — A transfer occasionally debits the wrong amount. This damages money and must be fixed now, a high-severity, high-priority defect, so the bank needs triage logic that treats this as the most urgent.

In the mini-project we build a defect triage model that stores severity and priority as separate fields, computes a triage recommendation, and sorts the defect queue so that business priority drives the fix order while severity is preserved for engineering context. We define a `Severity` enum, a `Priority` enum, a `Defect` with both fields plus affected-user count and workaround flag, and a `TriageService` that sorts by priority and explains each surprising combination.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four defects, each carrying an independent severity and priority plus affected-user count and a workaround flag.

Step 1: The triage service explains each defect. For the homepage typo it sees trivial severity but P1 priority and reports the divergence: nothing is broken, but fifty thousand visitors see a brand embarrassment, so it is urgent.

Step 2: For the admin crash it sees critical severity but P4 priority and reports the opposite divergence: a serious crash, but only one user, with a workaround, so it is scheduled later.

Step 3: For the wrong-amount transfer it sees critical severity and P1 priority aligned, the most dangerous and most urgent.

Step 4: The service then sorts the queue by priority so engineers work P1 items first, regardless of severity. The homepage typo and the money bug rise to the top; the serious-but-rare admin crash sinks despite its high severity.

Step 5: The final output shows the fix order driven by business priority, with severity preserved alongside for engineering context.

Final output:

```

2026-10-30 09:14:07 [INFO] [BUG-103] CRITICAL / P1_IMMEDIATE -> aligned.
2026-10-30 09:14:07 [INFO] [BUG-104] TRIVIAL / P4_LOW -> aligned.
2026-10-30 09:14:07 [INFO] === Fix order (driven by business PRIORITY) ===
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Tester files defect
    │ sets SEVERITY (impact): CRITICAL/MAJOR/MINOR/TRIVIAL
    ▼
  Defect record { severity, priority, affectedUsers, workaround }
    │
    ▼
  Product owner triage
    │ sets PRIORITY (urgency) using severity + users + workaround + schedule
    ▼
  ┌─────────────── divergence check ───────────────┐
  │ TRIVIAL + P1 → homepage typo (brand urgency)    │
  │ CRITICAL + P4 → rare admin crash (workaround)    │
  │ CRITICAL + P1 → wrong transfer amount (fix now)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ▼
  orderForFixing(): sort by PRIORITY → P1 first
    ▼
  Developer fix queue (severity shown for context)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Severity and priority are two independent axes of a defect. Severity is the technical and business impact, how badly the defect breaks functionality, correctness, data, or safety, and it is normally set by the tester based on the nature of the failure. Priority is how urgently the defect must be fixed relative to everything else, and it is normally set by the product owner based on how many users are affected, whether there is a workaround, revenue and compliance impact, reputation, and the release schedule. Because impact and urgency are different questions, the two can point in opposite directions.

The classic low-severity, high-priority example is a misspelled company name or a wrong logo on the public landing page: technically nothing is broken so severity is trivial, but every visitor sees an embarrassing brand mistake, so the business wants it fixed within the hour, making priority the highest. The mirror image is a crash in a rarely used admin edge case: a crash is technically serious so severity is critical, but if only one internal user ever triggers it and a manual workaround exists, the business is comfortable scheduling it for a later sprint, so priority is low. Of course many bugs are aligned, a transfer debiting the wrong amount is both high severity and high priority and must be fixed immediately, while a cosmetic misalignment on a seldom-visited page is low on both.

At the National Bank of India I always kept the two as separate fields in the tracker, and in bug reports I captured the affected-user count and whether a workaround existed, because those are exactly the facts the product owner needs to set priority sensibly. I remember a release week where a homepage typo in the bank's name, technically trivial, was raised to top priority ahead of a genuinely critical but rarely hit admin crash, and being able to explain calmly why that ordering was correct, impact versus urgency, reassured the stakeholders. Keeping the axes separate stops two failure modes: polishing cosmetic issues while serious bugs wait, and panicking over a scary-sounding bug that does not actually affect anyone. Being able to defend a surprising combination with a concrete banking example is what shows an interviewer I genuinely understand the distinction rather than treating the two words as synonyms.
